title: Adversus Valentinianos
author: Tertullian

passages.original: nec utique dicemur ipsi nobis finxisse materias, quas tot iam uiri sanctitate et praestantia insignes, nec solum nostri antecessores sed ipsorum haeresiarcharum contemporales, instructissimis uoluminibus et prodiderunt et retuderunt, ut Iustinus, philosophus et martyr, ut Miltiades, ecclesiarum sophista, ut Irenaeus, omnium doctrinarum curiosissimus explorator, ut Proculus noster, uirginis senectae et Christianae eloquentiae dignitas, quos in omni opere fidei, quemadmodum in isto, optauerim adsequi. aut si in totum haereses non sunt, ut qui eas pellunt finxisse credantur, mentietur apostolus, praedicator illarum.
passages.english: Nor, certainly, will it be said that we have invented for ourselves the material, which so many men already, distinguished for holiness and excellence, not only our predecessors but contemporaries of the heresiarchs themselves, have both exposed and refuted in most learned volumes: such as Justin, philosopher and martyr; such as Miltiades, the sophist of the churches; such as Irenaeus, the most painstaking investigator of all doctrines; such as our own Proculus, the ornament of chaste old age and of Christian eloquence, whom I would wish to match in every work of the faith, as in this one. Or if heresies do not exist at all, so that those who drive them out may be believed to have invented them, then the apostle, who foretold them, will be lying.
passages.notes: "virginis senectae" is taken as 'chaste (virgin) old age'; the phrase is compressed and its exact sense uncertain. "Proculus" is presumably the Montanist Proculus (Proclus).

passages.original: Primus omnium [Ennius] poeta Romanus \'caenacula maxima ca.eIP simpliciter pronuntiauit, elati situs nomine uel quia Iouem illic epulantem legerat apud Homerum. sed haeretici quantas supernitates supernitatum et quantas sublimitates sublimitatum in habitaculum dei sui cuiusque suspenderint extulerint expanderint, mirum est. etiam creatori nostro Enniana caenacula in aedicularum disposita sunt forma.
passages.english: The very first Roman poet, [Ennius], spoke plainly of 'the vast upper rooms of heaven', either from the name for a lofty position or because he had read in Homer of Jupiter feasting there. But it is astonishing how many heights upon heights and how many loftinesses upon loftinesses the heretics have hung up, raised up and spread out as a dwelling for each one's god. Even for our Creator Ennian upper rooms have been arranged in the form of little chambers.
passages.notes: The quotation is garbled in the text ("caenacula maxima ca.eIP"); read as "caenacula maxima caeli", 'the vast upper rooms of heaven'. The bracketed [Ennius] is the edition's.

passages.original: Itaque omnes et forma et scientia peraequantur, facti omnes quod unusquisque; nemo aliud, quia alteri omnes. refunduntur in Nus omnes, in Homines, in Theletos, aeque feminae in Sigas, in Zoas, in Ecclesias, in Fortunatas, ut Ouidius Metamorphosis suas deleuisset, si hodie maiores cognouisset. exinde refecti sunt et constabiliti sunt, et in requiem ex ueritate compositi magno cum gaudii fructu hymnis patrem concinunt.
passages.english: And so all are made completely equal in both form and knowledge, all having become what each one is; none is anything different, because all are the others. They are all poured back into Nuses, into Anthropoi, into Theletoi; likewise the females into Sigai, into Zoai, into Ecclesiai, into Fortunatae, so that Ovid would have erased his Metamorphoses if he had known these greater ones today. After that they were restored and firmly established, and, settled in rest on the basis of truth, with great fruit of joy they sing hymns to the Father in chorus.
passages.notes: Nus (Mind), Homo (Man), Theletus (Perfect), Sige (Silence), Zoe (Life), Ecclesia (Church), Fortunata (Blessed: Makaria) are Valentinian aeon names, given here in Tertullian's plural forms.
